competency: Explain how temperature, water, light, humidity, altitude, soil and biotic factors influence vegetable production.

en.text: Temperature affects photosynthesis, respiration, transpiration, germination and flowering; the first three rise with temperature up to a point. Each vegetable has a minimum, optimum and maximum temperature: temperate crops need less heat, tropical crops more. Warm soil speeds germination, root growth and uptake. Below 10 °C tropical vegetables may suffer chilling injury, while biennials and some cool-season crops such as onion and carrot need a cold period (vernalization) before they flower.

en.text: Fresh vegetables are often 80–90 % water, and about 322 litres of water are needed for each kilogram of vegetable dry matter. Water is needed for germination, dissolving nutrients, photosynthesis, and cell division, enlargement and turgidity. Shortage at critical stages (germination, flowering, seed setting) or early in growth cuts yield; excess water damages seedlings, washes out nutrients, erodes soil, floods fields and favours disease.

en.text: Light drives photosynthesis: in full light plants grow vigorously with more chlorophyll; in reduced light they are paler, soft and watery. Day length and light quality change with season, altitude and latitude, and the length of the night controls flowering in many plants. Long-day plants flower when nights are short (under about 12 hours), short-day plants when nights are long (over about 12 hours), and day-neutral plants under any light period.

en.text: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. Moderate humidity keeps stomata open for photosynthesis; very high humidity favours fungal diseases and slows transpiration, so leaves cool less; low humidity raises transpiration and can favour some pests. Altitude decides temperature and rainfall: temperature falls about 0.6 °C for every 100 m rise. Ethiopia's cool, rainy highlands are often suitable for vegetables; the hotter, drier lowlands are less suitable.

en.text: Soil type, fertility and structure affect growth and yield; soil gives roots nutrients, water and support. Texture is the particle size: sand is biggest, silt medium, clay smallest. Sandy soils have large pores, good air and free drainage but store little water; clay soils drain slowly and can waterlog. Compacted soil slows emergence, so seedlings stay longer exposed to pests. Biotic factors — bacteria, fungi, nematodes, viruses, weeds and animals — limit yield, so choose adapted, resistant crops.

notes.text: p.8: the book says excessive humidity closes stomata and so overheats plants. Overheating under high humidity comes mainly from slower transpiration (less evaporative cooling); stomata tend to close under low humidity/water stress. The lesson teaches the corrected reason.

Table 1.2 (humidity, p.9) comes from storage-humidity sources: in storage onion needs LOW and potato HIGH humidity, so both look misplaced. Two different tables are numbered "Table 1.2" (p.9 and p.12). Onion and potato are not used in graded humidity items.

Table 1.1: potato is usually short-day for tuber formation, and onion bulbing is long-day only in temperate varieties (many tropical onions are short-day). Kept as printed; potato and onion are not used in graded day-length items.

p.8: "Flowering and seed production by the length of the night is an example" is a fragment (meaning: night length triggers flowering). "Succulent" in the text means soft, watery tissue, unlike the cactus key term. p.7: "For example, excess moisture…" does not illustrate the shortage sentence.
p.10: "water lodging" should be "waterlogging"; "increases a time" should be "increases the time"; sandy soils have larger pores but less total pore space than clay.
Added: the 0.6 °C worked example, the tomato water-budget steps, the balanced photosynthesis equation, the factor–effect match and the challenges.
